subject: Art & Design
title: Realism: Painting the Unvarnished Truth
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Realism: Painting the Unvarnished Truth.

hook.text: Gustave Courbet painted peasants at actual size — the same scale reserved for kings and gods.

buildup.text: Realism rejected both Romantic drama and classical idealization. It showed life as it was.

discovery.text: Courbet's 'The Stone Breakers' depicted backbreaking labor with no moral or heroic framing.

twist.text: Critics called it ugly and vulgar. Courbet said: 'Show me an angel and I'll paint one.'

climax.text: Realism paved the way for every modern movement that valued truth over beauty.

punchline.text: Courbet didn't beautify the world. He dared to just show it.

quiz.question: What was radical about Courbet's Realism?
options: He painted ordinary people at the grand scale of kings

details.summary: Realism (1840s-1880s) depicted ordinary life without idealization. Gustave Courbet painted peasants and laborers at monumental scale previously reserved for gods and kings. Realists rejected Romantic fantasy and academic convention, insisting that art should show the world as it actually appeared.
details.whyItMatters: Realism democratized art's subject matter. By painting workers, poverty, and daily routines, it declared that ordinary lives deserve the same artistic attention as mythology and royalty — a revolutionary social statement through artistic choice.
takeaways: Depicted ordinary life without idealization or fantasy
Courbet painted laborers at monumental scale reserved for royalty
Declared ordinary lives deserve serious artistic attention

faq.question: What made Realism controversial?
faq.answer: Academic tradition held that only historical, mythological, and religious subjects deserved large-scale treatment. Courbet's massive painting of ordinary stone breakers at a scale usually reserved for kings was seen as a deliberate political provocation — and it was.

faq.question: How did Realism influence later art movements?
faq.answer: Realism's commitment to depicting contemporary life directly inspired Impressionism, which took the same subjects but focused on visual perception. Social Realism, documentary photography, and even Warhol's Pop Art all trace their roots to Courbet's insistence on painting the modern world.
